A decoy vault is a second, fully separate vault unlocked with a different password.

Use case: if someone forces you to open Pass Tech (border, assault, control), you give the decoy password. The app then shows a fake vault — it is cryptographically impossible to prove the real one exists.

Keep in mind:
• The decoy password must differ from the real one
• Fill the decoy with a few credible entries
• Biometric unlock will be turned off, and stays off for as long as a decoy exists: the fingerprint opens the real vault directly, which would defeat the decoy

Setting up a decoy vault will turn off biometric unlock. The fingerprint opens the real vault directly, so it would defeat the decoy in the very situation the decoy is for. You can still unlock with your master password.

resources.string: Someone close to you can reach the vault after a long period of inactivity. No cloud, no third party.
Tap to update the snapshot or turn it off

A password of its own, different from yours, lets someone close to you (partner, child, executor) reach the contents of the vault **after a long period of inactivity** on your part (90 days by default, plus 7 days of grace).

Keep in mind:
• The heir password must differ from your master password
• Give it to your heir safely (in person, in a will, in a bank vault) — it is never stored and cannot be recovered
• The heir reads a snapshot of the vault. Remember to update it from time to time.
• If you unlock the vault before the grace ends, the countdown starts again.
• All three snapshots then exist and look alike: nothing says which of your vaults the real one belongs to. That an heir is set up on this phone does show to an examination — for deniability, see the decoy vault.

This works entirely on the phone, with no cloud and no trusted third party.
Heir set up ✓ Vault snapshot encrypted.
The vault is empty — nothing to pass on

The heir reads a snapshot of the vault. You can:

• Update the snapshot (with the heir password)
• Turn inheritance off and delete the snapshot

Reads the domain shown by the browser in front, to check that it matches the Pass Tech entry before a password is copied. Only the domain is read, in memory only: nothing is stored and nothing is sent. Only recognised browsers are read. This is turned on at your request, and disappears from this list when you turn it off in Pass Tech.
Compares the browser\'s domain with those the entry declares
On — warns when the browser is not on the right domain

Pass Tech can check that the browser in front is on the entry's domain BEFORE copying your password, and warn you when it is not — a look-alike name, a fake site.

For that it uses an Android accessibility service:
• it reads the domain from the address bar, and nothing else
• only on recognised browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Edge, Opera, Vivaldi, Samsung, DuckDuckGo)
• nothing is stored, nothing is sent

Turning it off here takes the permission back: the service leaves Android's accessibility list, and turning it on again asks you for it.

On the next screen, turn "%1$s" on.

The only two times it uses the network

Asking GitHub whether a newer version has been published, once your vault is open, %1$d times a day at most. And the breach check on the audit screen, which you start yourself: the password itself is never sent, only the first five characters of its fingerprint, which tens of thousands of other passwords share.

Nothing else ever leaves this phone, and your vault least of all. What these two calls do show is that someone on your connection uses this app — GitHub sees a request for this project's latest release, and Have I Been Pwned sees five characters of a fingerprint.

AES-256-GCM. The key is derived from your master password by Argon2id (%1$d MiB of memory, %2$d passes) and by a key held in the phone\'s secure chip, which takes part in every single attempt.
The key lives in the Android Keystore and cannot be read without your fingerprint. It never leaves the phone, and a copy of the vault taken elsewhere cannot use it.
